Field surveys of West African ilisha along the coastal waters of the Gulf of Guinea indicate that this clupeiform species exhibits a moderate body size, with the largest individuals attaining a standard length of 30 centimeters [Li = 30 centimeters]. This ultimate length is comparable to that observed in other members of the Pristigasteridae family inhabiting similar estuarine environments. Growth trajectories derived from length-frequency data suggest that the species follows a relatively rapid early growth phase, with sexual maturation occurring well before the maximum size is achieved. Specifically, the standard length at which the onset of reproductive activity is first detected corresponds to approximately 13 cm [Lp = approximately 13 cm], a threshold that marks the transition from the juvenile stage to the reproductively viable adult phase. This length at puberty implies that individuals begin allocating resources toward gonadal development after having attained roughly 40 percent of their ultimate potential length, a pattern commonly documented in short-lived, fast-growing marine teleosts subject to high natural mortality rates. The relatively modest size at maturity, combined with a protracted spawning season, likely reflects an adaptive response to the variable productivity of the coastal upwelling systems that define this species' primary habitat.

Detailed histological examination of ovarian tissue from gravid females has provided valuable insight into the reproductive output of this species. When maintained at a stable water temperature of 27.5 °C [T = 27.5 °C], captive females produce approximately 1 to 3 eggs per batch [N_R_i = approximately 1 to 3 eggs per batch], with a spawning frequency of roughly 25 batches per year [F_R_i = roughly 25 batches per year]. The daily reproductive rate derived from these two sub-expressions corresponds to a maximum estimated output that has been observed under optimal feeding conditions in the laboratory, underscoring the species' potential for rapid population turnover when environmental conditions are favorable. Field validation of these laboratory-derived rates remains ongoing, as natural populations face variable food availability and predation pressure that may modulate actual reproductive performance in the wild.

The early life history of West African ilisha begins with the fertilised ovum, a pelagic, transparent, yolk-laden egg approximately 2.79 millimeters in diameter, which upon examination reveals a dry weight at birth of 0.0114 grams [Wwb = 0.0114 grams]. This minute initial mass is typical of pelagic-spawning teleosts that produce large numbers of small offspring as a bet-hedging strategy against high larval mortality in the planktonic environment. Under controlled laboratory conditions at 27.5 °C [T = 27.5 °C], the period between fertilisation and the hatching event is remarkably brief, lasting only 5 days [ab = only 5 days]. This rapid embryonic development, culminating in chorion rupture and the emergence of a yolk-sac larva, aligns with the thermal regime typical of tropical West African coastal waters where temperatures hover near the observed experimental value. The resulting prolarva, still dependent on endogenous yolk reserves, measures only a few millimeters in length and must quickly exhaust its lecithotrophic resources before transitioning to exogenous feeding. The yolk-sac stage is consequently short, placing a premium on the timely availability of suitable planktonic prey items such as copepod nauplii for the newly hatched, free-swimming larva.

As the larvae progress through the pelagic larval phase and undergo larval metamorphosis, they gradually increase in body mass, and by the time puberty is reached, the wet weight at this developmental milestone is recorded at 15 grams [Wwp = 15 grams]. This value, derived from the length-weight relationship specific to the species, represents the typical body mass at which first gonadal recrudescence is observed. In contrast, fully grown, reproductively active adults can attain a markedly larger ultimate wet weight of 191 grams [Wwi = 191 grams], a figure that reflects the substantial somatic growth achieved between the onset of sexual maturation and the attainment of asymptotic body size. The pronounced difference between the weight at puberty and the ultimate weight suggests that a considerable portion of the species' lifetime growth occurs during the adult phase, a pattern that is consistent with an indeterminate growth strategy common among tropical clupeiforms. This post-maturation growth is likely fueled by the high productivity of the coastal upwelling ecosystems, which provide a rich foraging environment for planktivorous fishes. The length-weight relationship underlying these estimates was validated using extensive field samples collected across multiple seasons, confirming the robustness of the allometric equation employed.

At a typical thermal regime of 27.5 °C [T = 27.5 °C], the maximum documented longevity under natural conditions reaches 6 years [am = 6 years]—a relatively compressed lifespan compared to many other marine teleosts and typical of small-bodied, fast-growing clupeiforms that experience high natural mortality rates from predation and fishing pressure. The age at birth, determined from controlled laboratory incubations at the same temperature, is notably brief at only 5 days [ab = only 5 days], accelerating the transition from the vulnerable egg stage to the free-swimming larval phase at a temperature of 27.5 °C [T = 27.5 °C]. Field data from tagging studies corroborate the estimated maximum lifespan, with the oldest recaptured individuals consistently falling within the 5- to 6-year age class. This limited longevity, coupled with the high reproductive output achieved through multiple spawning bouts per year, suggests that population persistence in West African ilisha is heavily dependent on consistent annual recruitment success rather than the survival of a few long-lived individuals.
